changes.after: Add a database field while keeping the records that already exist.

before: A migration changes an existing database schema without pretending it is a fresh empty database.
Dropping and recreating a table may erase saved data. Adding a column can preserve rows when that change fits the database’s supported rules.
A default tells existing rows what value to use for the new field. Here unfinished notes should begin with done equal to 0.

This separate example adds a column.
```sql
ALTER TABLE tasks ADD COLUMN archived INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;
```
A schema version records which migration has been applied. SQLite offers user_version as an application-controlled integer.
If a migration fails, the application should roll back rather than report the new version as complete. Test the failure path before changing real stored data.
This fixture starts at version 1. The exercise runs once in a new isolated database; running the same ADD COLUMN twice is not an automatic no-op.
A production migration runner checks the current version, applies the next supported change, and records success. It also needs a tested backup and recovery plan.
After migration, verify the old IDs and titles, the default values, and the new version.
after: A schema describes a database's tables and columns. A migration is a planned change to that schema. It must account for records that are already saved.
Dropping and rebuilding a table can erase its rows. ALTER TABLE can add a supported new column while preserving the existing data.
DEFAULT gives old rows a value for the new field. NOT NULL requires a known value. Here, 0 means the old task is not archived.
SQLite's user_version is a number the application controls. It records which schema change has been completed. It does not perform the change itself.
A transaction groups related database changes. BEGIN starts it, and COMMIT makes its changes final. Keep the added column and version update in the same successful transaction.
If a migration fails, its runner should roll back the unfinished transaction. Do not report version 2 as installed when the needed column was not successfully added.
This exercise starts with version 1 in a fresh, isolated database. Run its change once. Adding the same column twice is an error, not an automatic no-change operation.
A real upgrade runner checks the current version before choosing a migration. Test the upgrade and recovery with a backup before applying it to important stored data.

Migrate the supplied notes table by adding done INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0. Preserve every old ID and title. Set user_version to 2 in the same successful transaction, then check the old rows and new default values.

before.question: A migration fails before its transaction commits. Why must the runner avoid reporting version 2 as successfully installed?
choices: Later code could assume a schema change that never completed.
Version numbers automatically repair missing columns.
A failed migration deletes every backup.
before.explanation: A version marker is evidence of completed schema work. Advancing it separately can make future code skip a change the database still needs.

after.question: A migration fails before commit. Why must the runner avoid reporting version 2 as installed?
choices: Later code could expect a change that never completed
The version number repairs missing columns
A failed migration deletes every backup
after.explanation: The version must describe completed work, or later code may rely on a missing column.

changes.before: Only the isolated SQLite fixture is migrated. This lesson does not change any live database. Real migration systems need version checks, backups, rollback/recovery tests and toolchain-specific transaction behavior.
changes.after: Only an isolated SQLite database is changed in the browser. A real migration needs version checks and tested backup and recovery steps.
